[music] Scott, great to see you. >> Good to see you, Ted. >> I know we're going to talk a lot about continuation funds. Why don't we start with your background and path to the seat? >> Born and raised in Texas. I went to university in Texas, had an internship at Enron the summer that it all went wrong. Had an incredible experience, had an offer, but decided I wanted to move to New York. I wanted to work on Wall Street. I turned it down. I'm glad I did because by the end of that year, Enron was no more. That was a formidable experience for me. I wanted to be a stock picker. I interviewed around, I networked, I got an offer with Morgan Stanley to join their equity research team. This was in the fall of 2001. The dotcom bubble had just burst. Around Christmas break, I got a call saying unfortunately massive layoffs, the economy is not good. We can no longer honor that offer. I said, oh, I was looking forward to having fun my last semester in college and now I'm jobless. I moved to New York and I joined the litigation consulting business of PwC. I got to see a lot of interesting frauds as a forensic accountant. I always had at the back of my head this itch to get back and be a stock picker. Low and behold, 2004 came around. Two years later, I got a call back from Morgan Stanley and they said, market's different. Can we talk? I got an offer to join Morgan Stanley. They stuck the Texan on the energy team. I had grew up in suburban Dallas, Texas, never seen the oil well in my life. I loved it. That's how I got into investing. Quickly over the course of my two years as a stock picker, I realized three key things. First, I quickly realized I wanted to be on the buy side, not the sell side. I wanted to be making investments, not making investment recommendations. The second one, I decided public markets may not be for me. I would get in early, work all hours into the night, early morning, submit a final research report after the earnings came out to my boss. We'd publish our report nobody cared. The market had moved hours and hours before. I quickly realized I'm more of a longer-term fundamentals type investor which to me signaled private equity might be the right way to go. The third piece I had to figure out is did I want to be a GP or an LP? And this was in 2006. The LP industry was much smaller than it is today. I started doing as much research as I could. I started networking with as many people as I could. I learned a lot about LPs and what they do. I knew what GPs were. I lived in New York. I had roommates that worked at GPs. This is neither good or bad. I call a GP an inch wide and a mile deep. The more I learned about LPs, I decided they're an inch deep and a mile wide. For me and my own interest, skill sets, and intellectual curiosity, that sounded pretty interesting. I interviewed with anyone that I could. Ultimately got a job with Alpine West Partners. I spent four years with Alpine West, learned everything there is to know about being a private equity LP. Fell in love with the LP side of things. I also met a woman along the way. We got married while we lived up here in New York. She happened to be a fellow Texan. After spending eight years in the Northeast, both of us looked around, said what do we want to do at this next phase and where do we want to plant our roots? We decided for us that was going to be back home. In 2010, we packed up, left the city, moved to Austin, Texas, and I linked up with the Teacher Retirement System of Texas where I am to this day. I've been at TRS or Texas Teachers for 16 and 1/2 years. I focus exclusively on private equity. When I joined, the private equity portfolio was six people, $7 billion of NAV approximately. Fast forward over 16 years later, we're now 27 investment professionals on the private equity team, about $33 billion in NAV in private equity. It's been a fun ride. It's been a great time to be an LP in this industry. Today I lead the private equity funds team within Texas Teachers. >> What are some of the key lessons or inflection points? >> The first one was coming out in the dot com recession, having my dream job swept out from under my feet was a little bit of a blow to the ego, blow to the plan. I thought I had it all figured out. The world had a different plan for me. My lesson learned was that's okay. Life is sometimes not a straight line. It's a series of decisions. I still generated an incredible network from that first job, some great skills. I saw some cool stuff. Little bit of a different route than I had planned in my own head. The next key lesson was I was at Alpine Vest investing in private equity when the bubble burst in 2008 in the GFC. The lesson learned there was when others are pulling back, go in. 2009 ended up being an incredible vintage. 2010 was an incredible vintage, an incredible time to deploy capital. >> How about once you got in the seat taking a program from the size it was to the size of this today? >> That's been a lesson in Rome wasn't built in a day. I look back and think about how much our program has evolved. I was just a small piece of that evolution. Never once did any of us sit down on the team and say this is where we're going to be in 16 years. It was this is what we're going to do today. This is the next stop along our journey. We'd accomplish that and then say what's next. The Texas Teachers Program was built over a long period of time one step at a time. >> Did you look at your portfolio in the industry today? There's been this big exit bottleneck, continuation vehicles, perhaps not as well understood in the community as you would like. Would love to get your thoughts of how did you come about thinking through all the challenges in understanding what a CV means to an LP? >> Continuation vehicles, continuation funds, GP led secondaries, I'm a strong believer that they are neither inherently good or inherently bad. Each vehicle is unique and bespoke and requires examination on its own. With that comes some difficulties. If you go back when CVs took off the second wave 10 years ago, GPs treated it like a new invention. Historically there's been three ways to exit a business, an IPO, a sale to a sponsor, or a sale to a strategic. All of a sudden we had invented this fourth way. You would think LPs would be super excited by this, and GPs were. They were metaphorically high-fiving each other because they had just increased the exit routes by a third. As I looked around and evaluated these on my own, as our team evaluated them, as I talked to my fellow LPs, it quickly became apparent that LPs were not nearly as enthusiastic as GPs expected them to be. Recently, I've seen frustrations hit new highs. By chair of the board of ILPA, I spend a lot of time with some of the senior-most LPs in this industry. When I hear things like CVs are the bane of my existence, there's a joke now that CV stands for conflict vehicle. Some LPs say my heart sinks when a CV request lands in my inbox. I've even heard some say CVs are going to be the death of the industry. These are strong statements that clearly are not high-fiving the GPs for creating this fourth exit tool. I started to say LPs have strong emotions about this. GPs are not fully appreciating the nuance of the concerns. I started to write down some ideas as to how to articulate why LPs can be concerned about this. It started with the conflicted nature. That's where GPs thought that it started and ended. As I started jotting more and more down, I realized there's a lot more to this that GPs might value hearing beyond the conflicted nature of the transactions. I've come up with the top 10 reasons LPs are concerned about CVs. You and I were talking at a conference this summer, and I mentioned it. Here we are. >> Let's have at it. We don't have Letterman anymore, so it'll be the Scott Ramsey top 10 list. >> We'll start with one and go up to 10. The first reason LPs are concerned are exactly what GPs expected. These are conflicted transaction. There's conflicted pricing. There's imperfect price discovery. The GP sits on both sides of the trade. They act as the agent for the seller, which is the legacy LPs. Functionally, they also act as the agent for the buyer, which is the incoming CV investors. That makes it hard to know whether the price is real, whether a competitive process was run. That's the main and the original concern around LPs, around CVs is the conflicted nature of the transaction. >> Before we move on, now that that's been in the market for a while, what do you see as best practices in an inherently opaque pricing environment? >> ILPA has issued a 2.0 of continuation vehicles best practices. It's in the draft process collecting community input. It comes down to four things, one of which is pricing. The first is the rationale. Is there a genuine case that the CV is a deliberate solution as opposed to a default? Is this the best option that exists? The second one is the process. Was a truly competitive auction run? Did third party non-secondary buyers participate? Was there a process to seek a wholesale sale of these assets? Is there full price transparency around what the final bidders offered? For example, if one bidder is willing to pay 90 cents on the dollar for an asset, another bidder will pay 89 cents on the dollar, but commit to the GP's next fund. That's something LPs don't always have transparency into. Usually the LPAC just says this is the bid we've decided to go with. LPs are now requesting more transparency to prove is there more to the bid than just the headline pricing. In addition is to support the valuation as a third party fairness opinion. A lot of LPs say that those can have limited value. They're a important process check through it all. Finally is checking in on governance and alignment. Do the LPs get sufficient time to review the roll or sell decision? Are LPs economically neutral, meaning that they're no worse off from an economics perspective? Is the GP rolling its own carry? Full transparency into alignment. >> If you look at the totality of CVs that you've seen in your seat. Do you find the pricing fair in general? Is there a wide dispersion, heavily discounted? What should you expect when a CV lands on your desk? >> It's a complicated transaction. Every time we're talking about these internally, I'm learning something new. A lot of times the questions are similar. There's more bells and whistles getting added to all of these. LP is trying to help and come out with a standardized checklist for the GP to fill out. Did you do X? Did you do Y? Often times you have to peel back the onion. It's similar to a co-invest in a lot of ways. There's an asset. You have to form a view on that asset. Is it an asset you want to own or an asset you don't want to own? On top of that, something you don't have to do in a co-investment, but you do have to do in a CV is determine alignment. Almost always in a co-investment, you're fully aligned with the GP. You'll buy at the same terms, you'll sell at the same terms. If they win, you win. If you win, they win. That's not always the case with the CV. You have to understand where does the GP's alignment lie? What are they getting out of this transaction? What is the third party offer? Is that a fair price? >> We start with the obvious one that is more complex than it seems on the surface. Won't you bring me through the next nine? >> Beyond conflicted pricing. Number two, dilution of GP mindshare. Every hour a GP spends managing a CV is an hour they're not spending managing my co-mingled fund, the fund to which I committed capital. Well, I may be an investor in that CV, but if I'm not, I'm losing their mindshare. It's not a restricted only to CVs. There are other things that cause loss of GP mindshare, but it's one of the reasons that LPs can be concerned about these. The third reason would be dilution of alignment. A CV is a new economic vehicle that will bring in a new stream of revenues from management fees from carry. This opens the door for the GP to win even if the original fund loses. LPs are always trying to create scenarios of perfect alignment such that if LP loses, the GP loses, and if LP wins, GP wins. Continuing on, the fourth, LPs can potentially be paying worse economics for a deal they already owned. LPs have to take the time and focus to ensure that the management fee rate is the same, the headline percentage, the cost basis is unchanged. Carry shouldn't be at a higher rate than you would have otherwise paid in the fund. Rolling into a new CV should not be paying more to own the same asset. That's not always an easy calculation to do. The owner should be on the GP to ensure rolling LPs are no worse off. We call this in economics status quo. >> What are some of the ways that an LP might not fully understand they're going to be paying more rolling into a CV? >> Perfect example. Let's pretend we're in a fund. After the investment period, the management fee is 100 basis points, 1% on invested capital. Let's pretend the asset that they're going to sell to the CV they bought for $100. Us LPs would be paying 1% on $100 or a dollar a year. The CV may have 70 basis points as a headline management fee rate. 70 basis points, that's good. That's less than 1%. However, the second component of the management fee is crucial, which is what is the cost basis. The GP may be bought the asset originally at $100. They're going to sell it to the CV at $300. Your new cost basis is $300. But LP is now paying 70 basis points on $300, which is higher than 100 basis points on $100. That's on the management fee. On the carry, the market can differ. Often times there's tiered carry. We've seen structures such that carry can end up being higher than the original fund. The fifth one is more complex than a lot realize. Many LPs don't have a choice to roll. While GPs present CVs as you make the call, stay, or you can sell. It's your choice, LPs. A lot of LPs for a variety of reasons don't have that choice. They may have a board approval process that takes longer than the CV process allows for. They may have a legal review or no bandwidth from their legal team to do a legal review. The election windows oftentimes can be short, 20 to 30 business days. They might have a plate full of other priorities to get done. While it's presented as a choice, a lot of LPs don't have a choice. As a result, their only option is to sell. That's concerning. The sixth one, CVs can artificially enhance fund metrics. The original commingled fund, when it sells a CV to a new vehicle, it produces DPI and an IRR for that fund. Even though the asset is ongoing and the GP is still managing it, it has locked in DPI and IRR for the fund, even though the true value creation is not yet done. As a result, the GP's track record arguably is improved through this conflicted transaction. LPs can walk into our investment committee and present higher DPIs than perhaps our investment committee realizes. We'll show it both ways, actual DPI and DPI less, we call it synthetic DPI when it's a CV or an NAV loan. We'll strip all of that out. >> In an instance where you see a CV that you feel is a trophy asset, the classic asset that a GP wants to hold on for longer because it performs well and there's lots more to do, when you go to re-underwrite a manager, if you've stripped that out as part of synthetic DPI, how do you think about the difference between that CV versus another CV that you might not feel strongly about the quality of the asset? >> We show full track record, which includes all the funds plus all the CVs when we walk into our investment committee. It's almost a no win when we show the CV track record. If you walk in with a CV track record that's too good, you would think they'd be excited because it is still a investment judgment and our investment committee is upset because they think if it did that well, they sold it for too cheap and therefore a fair process wasn't run. If you walk in with a bad CV track record, the investment committee says, what's wrong with this GP? They have bad investment judgment. Why did they continue to own this asset? There's not a CV track record that can win in terms of an investment committee. With that, by definition, CVs can't outperform too much. They're exceptions to the rule. The asset class as a whole, the subsector of CVs. If they start doing too well, LPs will stop allowing GPs to do these out of the original fund. If they start doing too poorly, LPs will stop funding the CV buyers. There's a healthy tension such that CVs by their nature can't be structurally too good, also can't be structurally too bad. There's not much data on performance out there, it's early. The data I've seen supports that that's the case. Number seven. LPs are paying for an exit function that's no longer being performed. As LPs, we pay a GP by and large two and 20 to use the generic terms. What are we paying two and 24? There's three key judgment items that the GP does that we're paying for. The first is sourcing and evaluating investments. The second is creating value in those investments. The third is exiting those investments. If you take CVs to their logical extreme, and a GP CVs every asset in its fund, it's thrown its hands up on the third and said, I'm conflicted. I can no longer make the exit determination. LP, it's your decision. That's fine, but I paid UGP to do three things. You're only doing two of those. That's frustrating because us limited partners are becoming less limited. We're not paying any less for taking the decision making back within our own teams. >> What's the potential to renegotiate that fee? >> This is one of those idealistic statements. I've yet to hear anyone say, that's unfair. It takes a long time to change markets. There is an entire infrastructure built around the two and 20 model. I'm not sitting here proposing that we're going to change that overnight. It's more highlighting to a GP. Here's one of many reasons. It's a shifting of the discernment that an LP is paying a GP for. >> How about the last three? >> Number eight, cannibalization of co-investment. Historically, if this asset had been sold to another GP, probably that other GP would have required some co-invest to do it. The market for buyout co-investment, at least in the US, is no fee, no carry. This is effectively been taken out of the co-invest pipeline. This is effectively cannibalizing fee-free co-invest because now it's fee-paying co-invest via a CV vehicle. LPs have built a lot of infrastructure up over the last couple of decades around building out co-invest teams. This is taking some of the deals out of the pipeline. Understandably, that's frustrating. >> Have you seen that in practice that the co-investment top of the funnel is less than you would have thought? >> I've seen a couple of things. First, deals that have gone into CVs we know historically we're not IPOs, we're not strategic candidates. They would have been sold to another sponsor. They would have been too t big for that sponsor. That is absolutely happening. Some co-investments that I've heard from LPs when they're exiting alongside the fund, they might be allowed to reinvest, but it's via the CV at full fees. Even if you had a co-invest in the original and the GP is going to keep the asset through a CV, that fee-free co-invest option is being taken away. LPs are being forced to either exit what they had at no fee, no carry, or roll it into now a worse fee structure than they had before, full fees, full carry. Number nine, reduction of right tail upside. These are often pitched as a GP's best assets. Often times we'll see CVs created when an asset has reached a 3x or a 5x, maybe even a 7 or a 10x multiple within the fund. The GP says it's time to de-risk this fund and put it into a CV. That makes sense. However, most CVs I've seen are underwritten to at least another 2x. This is an asset that was sold at a 5x out of the fund is being underwritten at a 2x in a CV. Had that stayed in the original fund, that would have been a 10x deal. That's the exact reason that LPs are in the private equity business is the ability to capture that right tail skew when these best performing assets get moved down into the system. That can be frustrating for an LP who doesn't get to benefit from that. >> The last on the list. >> The final one, number 10, is somewhat related to number nine. If you take that last philosophy and you apply it across the whole industry, CVs could have downward pressure on private equity returns industry wide. These best assets are being systematically taken out of commingled funds and moved into standalone CVs before their final exit and before the full value creation story is over. The data suggests LPs are selling more than they're rolling. The LPs who are typically only exposed to the original fund, are not getting the benefit of those higher outside returns. >> Cuz you've laid out these ten, imagine some theoretical, most practical limitations of CVs. You're also actively managing this program that's going to have these CVs landing on all your desks all the time. Knowing what you know about this, how have you chosen to participate in the market? >> We've chosen to participate in two ways. First, we sit on the advisory board of almost every fund that we invest in. We take a hands-on role as an advisory board member in terms of evaluating these CVs in order to waive the conflict. We've developed a scorecard internally that we fill out has a GP done X, has a GP done Y. If not, we vote no. The second then is when we have the opportunity to roll or sell ourselves when the election notice comes out. We've taken the view that as long as it's over a certain size threshold, we have a $250 billion planet Texas teachers. Some things are not enough capital to be a good use of time. When it's over a certain size threshold, we have to roll up our sleeves and dig in. We're evaluating the asset. We're evaluating the sponsor fit. All that's the same work as a co-investment. We're also evaluating the alignment. That can be a lot harder to do. We have to effectively stop everything we're doing and evaluate it. We 've also decided we have a large dedicated co-investment team. We've opened up the phone lines to be buyers of CVs that are beyond our roll sell decisions. We're actively out there sourcing new deals, evaluating those. They do have a higher bar because they have fees associated with them relative to most of our co-invest deal flow, which is no fee, no carry. We have a certain threshold upon which we might be willing to accept some fees in a CV if we like the asset. We've had to build out the resources, roll up our sleeves. We found no other way around it. >> To To a sense, within the CVs that come from your existing portfolio of managers that fit that minimum size threshold, what percentage of them would you say you end up investing or rolling in? >> It's a number that we track. It's not a number that we publicize publicly. However, of the actionable deals we see, we call it a hit rate. How many do we do versus how many do we exit or sell? Our hit rate is no different in CV roll versus sell decisions as it is in actionable co-investment decisions. If we do one out of 10 co-invest, we probably do one out of 10 rolls. We don't have a house view that CVs are inherently good or bad, a great buy or a great sell. Interesting opportunities can exist, but you have to do the work. >> Should we take a step back from CVs as this fourth leg of a stool of how GPs are going to get liquidity? We're still facing this liquidity bottleneck that's been around since the last four or five years. How do you think this is playing out over the next couple of years? >> It's something we spent a lot of time thinking about. It's something we're concerned about. It brings me to a topic we haven't covered but probably should, which is zombie funds. A zombie fund is a fund that has stopped making new deals, also can't raise capital. It's neither dead because the fund still has assets in it. It's not alive either because they're not adding to those assets and they have no more dry powder. It's a zombie. We saw them a lot coming out of five years or so post financial crisis. The industry data suggests other LPs have the same view that these zombie funds are going to become a real industry problem in the coming years. I saw a research report by Caller this summer come out and say that 54% of LPs expect the number of zombie funds in their portfolio two years from now to be higher. Two years ago, that number was 28%. There's a structural vintage problem. The 2018 to 2022 vintages deployed capital in a low rate, high multiple environment. They were not able to exit those deals in time. That environment no longer exists. The math doesn't work on exits. As a result, there's a structural DPI problem. That backlog is going to take years to work through the system. CVs are an interesting topic because you would think that they would solve the zombie problem. All CVs do is kick this can down the road. A CV can help an individual asset. It might help a single GP avoid being a zombie. There's far more stranded assets than there is capital for CVs. CVs alone will not solve the zombie problem. This cash becomes trapped earning limited returns, if any. You can't exit without selling in the secondary market at a significant discount. All the while, the economics are misaligned. A GP is collecting fees on NAV or on their cost basis that hasn't converted the cash in years. There's little incentive for them to force a sale because they may not be in the carry. There may not be any more cash coming in when they sell. These funds are often amongst us LPs worst performers. They become a huge drag on your time from a governance perspective. Lots of amendments come our way. I don't have an answer to your question, Ted, on how the liquidity drought gets solved. It's going to force some knock on effects such as zombie funds that are going to start taking the mind share of us LPs and start to become a real frustrating topic for us all to deal with. >> What do you hear about the public markets, the IPO market as a potential exit path for private equity assets? >> Outside of a couple large scale growth capital names, we haven't seen a lot of activity in the public markets. We're not encouraging our GPs to go and exit through the public markets because it can often be hard for them to fully exit. I call an IPO step one of a multi-step exit because rarely can you get full liquidity on day one. >> The other big question in people's minds in private equity is what happens with private wealth, retail retirement plan assets coming in. Wondering if you have any views of where we are today and where that might go in the future. >> This has been an emerging concern. LPs are watching it closely. A lot of the top 10 concerns we just walked through on CVs are the exact same concerns LPs have on private wealth and retail capital. Some of the same ones are dilution of the GP's time and attention, dilution of the alignment because of this new fee stream, co-invest cannibalization. What's interesting about retail capital, it's a unique wrinkle to this versus CVs. There's a saying out there that I like, which is private equity for the retail investor is the right strategy but the wrong structure. Institutional investors, people like Texas teachers, and retail investors, people like myself, my parents' 401k plan, we have different risk profiles, liquidity needs, time horizons, performance expectations, level of expertise and resources. Yet a retail product oftentimes those retail investors are being placed in the exact same assets side by side with an institutional investor. One of private equity's advantages over public markets was that companies can stay focused on the long term. Putting these into a semi-liquid quarterly redemption vehicle takes away that long-term horizon. Illiquidity is a feature, not a bug of the private equity asset class. You're taking away that feature, in my opinion, when you put it into a semi-liquid structure. >> What are some of the >> other things you have your eyes on? >> Within retail, the things that we care about in addition to some of the top ten items, we're paying a lot of attention to hard caps and sharing percentage. How much can a commingled fund share with a retail vehicle alongside it? If I go into a $10 billion fund, I'm not paying attention to the LPA. If that LPA allows a retail vehicle to invest infinite amounts, then I've effectively signed up for an uncapped fund. Fund size is a key underwriting of SLPs. Knowing how much they can invest is a key care about. Another one is, how does the investment timing work? Are both the retail and the institutional fund required to buy and sell at the same time? Can one buy and sell to the other? Can one sell before the other? There are inherent conflicts, different risk tolerances, liquidity needs between two different investors. Finally, is this cannibalizing our co-investment opportunity? We're spending a lot of time thinking about these things. >> So far, most of the activity, to the extent there is activity on the retail side with private equity has started with the large, mostly public alternative asset managers. Curious if you've seen traction below that top tier of half a dozen firms. >> We haven't seen a lot start to raise products. When I talk with a lot of our GPs, if you catch them in a moment of truth and transparency, they would say they're certainly thinking about it. Met with a large, publicly traded CEO recently. This individual said, sure I'm glad I'm CEO of a large firm and not a small firm right now because of the strength of consolidation that this large cap manager has. I'm not sure that it's coming immediately to the middle market. However, eventually, if it continues to grow, large cap players will want middle market offerings for their retail investors. They'll need distribution channels, a pipeline of assets to take advantage of the new capital coming in that has appetite for smaller deals. You may see joint ventures, you may see consolidation of GPs, you may see the big buying the smaller. So while it's not there now, there's a world in which it could be far more prevalent for middle market GPs down the road. >> What's changed in the last few years in how you've gone about investing in the space? >> We're spending a lot more time now than we would have on a couple of areas. One is we are underwriting the unrealized portfolio more deeply than we had in the past. It was easy to assume when markets were up and to the right that a deal held at cost would get to 2 X. That's harder to assume now. We're spending a lot of time understanding what was the multiple paid for this portfolio. How has EBITDA traded? How has revenue performed since entry?
